## Appendix C Theoretical Proofs

### C.1 Proof of [Theorem 1](#Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")

We first introduce an episodic version of performance difference lemma
\[[Kakade and Langford, 2002](#bib.bib32)\].

###### Lemma 2 (Performance difference lemma).

For any policy $`\pi^{\prime}`$ and $`\pi`$, we have

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{J}(\pi^{\prime})-\mathcal{J}(\pi)=\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\prime}}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-V_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h})\right]
``` |  |

Let $`f_{h}`$ be any function, then from
[Lemma 2](#A3.Ex6 "Lemma 2 (Performance difference lemma). ‣ C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
we have

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\pi^{\star})-\mathcal{J}({\widehat{\pi}})=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-V_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h})\right]`$ |  | (4) |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~+\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi^{\star}}_{h}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]\right]`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~+\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi^{\star}}_{h},a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})\right].`$ |  |  |

Let
$`f_{h}(s_{h},a_{h})\coloneqq\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-c(s_{h})`$,
where
$`c(s_{h})={\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$,
then

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\pi^{\star})-\mathcal{J}({\widehat{\pi}})=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right]`$ |  | (I) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~+\beta\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}}}\Bigg[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]\Bigg]`$ |  | (II) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~+\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right].`$ |  | (III) |

For term I, from Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left|Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right|\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sqrt{H\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}`$ |  |

From
[Assumption 1](#S3.EGx1 "Assumption 1 (Coverage). ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |

We now introduce the following lemma to further bound term I.

###### Lemma 3.

Under
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2 (In-distribution reward learning). ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we have for any $`h\in\{0,1,\cdots,H-1\}`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}{2},`$ |  |

where
$`c(s_{h})={\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$.

Then from
[Lemma 3](#Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 3. ‣ C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
we know

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~\sqrt{H\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sqrt{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}H\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}+c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~H\sqrt{\frac{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}{2}}`$ |  |

Similarly, term III can be bounded as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sqrt{H\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~\sqrt{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}H\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{{\widehat{\pi}}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]}`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~H\sqrt{\frac{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}{2}}`$ |  |

Now, let’s consider term II. Given a fixed $`h`$ and fixed $`s_{h}`$,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{y\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]+{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{\pi^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{\pi^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\|{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}[{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\|\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})]`$ |  |

From
[Assumption 1](#S3.EGx1 "Assumption 1 (Coverage). ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{\pi^{\star}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\|{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}[{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})\|\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\leq`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log C_{\mathcal{A}}\right]-0-0`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\log C_{\mathcal{A}}`$ |  |

Therefore, with
$`\beta\leq\frac{\sqrt{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}}{\log C_{\mathcal{A}}}`$,
term II can be bounded as

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\beta\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}}}\Bigg[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim{\widehat{\pi}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}\right]\Bigg]\leq\beta H\log C_{\mathcal{A}}=H\sqrt{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}`$ |  |

In conclusion,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}(\pi^{\star})-\mathcal{J}({\widehat{\pi}})=O\left(H\sqrt{C_{\mathcal{S}}^{\star}C_{\mathcal{A}}\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}\right)
``` |  |

### C.2 Proofs for Supporting Lemmas

Proof of
[Lemma 2](#A3.Ex6 "Lemma 2 (Performance difference lemma). ‣ C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
Let us prove by induction. When $`H=1`$, the trajectory consists of a
single step, and the statement is trivial.

Now assume that for horizon $`k`$ the statement holds for any policy
$`\pi^{\prime}`$ and $`\pi`$:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}_{k}(\pi^{\prime})-\mathcal{J}_{k}(\pi)=\sum_{h=1}^{k}\mathbb{E}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\prime}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})-V_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h})\right].
``` |  |

For $`H=k+1`$, we expand
$`\mathcal{J}_{k+1}(\pi^{\prime})-\mathcal{J}_{k+1}(\pi)`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{k+1}(\pi^{\prime})-\mathcal{J}_{k+1}(\pi)=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}}\left[\sum_{h=2}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[V_{2}^{\pi}(s_{2})]`$ |  | (I) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~+{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[r(s_{1},a_{1})]+{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[V_{2}^{\pi}(s_{2})]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$ |  | (II) |

Term I corresponds to the difference between expected returns of
$`\pi^{\prime}`$ and $`\pi`$ on an MDP with horizon $`k`$. Apply the
inductive hypothesis to term I, we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{\prime}}\left[\sum_{h=2}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]-{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi}^{\prime}[V_{2}^{\pi}(s_{2})]=\sum_{h=2}^{H}\mathbb{E}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\prime}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[Q_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})-V_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h})\right]`$ |  |

For term II, we have

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[r(s_{1},a_{1})]+{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[V_{2}^{\pi}(s_{2})]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{h=1}^{k+1}r(s_{h},a_{h})\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi^{\prime}}[Q_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1},a_{1})]-{\mathbb{E}}_{\pi}[V_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1})]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{1}\sim d_{1}^{\pi^{\prime}}}\left[{\mathbb{E}}_{a_{1}\sim\pi^{\prime}(\cdot\mid s_{1})}\left[Q_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1},a_{1})\right]-V_{1}^{\pi}(s_{1})\right]`$ |  |

Summing up term I and II concludes our proof.

Proof of
[Lemma 3](#Thmtheorem3 "Lemma 3. ‣ C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h}),a_{h}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}^{\prime}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}^{\prime}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})+Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h}^{\prime})\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h}),a_{h}^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\Bigg[`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~\bigg(\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)-\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}^{\prime}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}^{\prime}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h}^{\prime})-c(s_{h})\right)\bigg)^{2}\Bigg]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~2{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle~-2{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h}}\left[\left({\mathbb{E}}_{a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right]\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle=`$ | $`\displaystyle~2{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]`$ |  |

The last step follows from the definition of $`c(s_{h})`$. Under
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2 (In-distribution reward learning). ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}_{h},a_{h}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[\left(\beta\log\frac{{\widehat{\pi}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(a_{h}\mid s_{h})}-Q_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-c(s_{h})\right)^{2}\right]\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathsf{stat}}}{2}`$ |  |

### C.3 Analysis of the Approximation of $`Q`$-Values

In this section, we analyze the $`Q`$-value approximation in practical
DPSDP described in
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Practical Algorithm ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection").
As only one feedback and refinement step is used during training, we
assume $`H=3`$. Let $`\hat{\pi}`$ be the resulting policy, and let
$`\widetilde{Q}_{h}^{\hat{\pi}}`$ denote the estimated $`Q`$-values,
replacing $`Q_{h}^{\hat{\pi}}`$ in
[Assumption 2](#Thmassumption2 "Assumption 2 (In-distribution reward learning). ‣ 3.2 Algorithm Analysis ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection").

We define advantage function as
$`A_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})=Q_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})-V_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h})`$,
and
$`\widetilde{A}_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})=\widetilde{Q}_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})-\mathbb{E}_{a_{h}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s_{h})}[\widetilde{Q}_{h}^{\pi}(s_{h},a_{h})]`$.
Then
[Eq. 4](#A3.E4 "In C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
can be rewritten as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}(\pi^{\star})-\mathcal{J}({\widehat{\pi}})=\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}{\mathbb{E}}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}\left[A_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})\right].`$ |  | (5) |

We analyze each term in
[Eq. 5](#A3.E5 "In C.3 Analysis of the Approximation of 𝑄-Values ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
as follows:

1.  1.
    At $`h=2`$, the estimated
    $`\widetilde{Q}_{2}^{{\widehat{\pi}}_{3}}(s_{2},a_{2})=r(s_{3})`$ is
    exact. Therefore,
    $`A_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})=\widetilde{A}_{h}^{\widehat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})`$.
2.  2.
    At $`h=1`$, the estimated $`Q`$-value is:
    $`\widetilde{Q}_{1}^{{\widehat{\pi}}_{2}}(s_{1},a_{1})=\mathbb{E}_{a_{2}\sim\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}(\cdot\mid s_{2})}[r(s_{3})]=Q_{1}^{\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}}(s_{1},a_{1})`$.
    We define the approximation error:

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \Delta=\mathbb{E}_{s_{h}\sim d_{h}^{\pi^{\star}},a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}[A_{h}^{\hat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})-\widetilde{A}_{h}^{\hat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})]
    ``` |  |
3.  3.
    At $`h=0`$, we have
    $`\widetilde{Q}_{0}^{\hat{\pi}_{1}}(s_{0},a_{0})=r(s_{1})+\frac{H-1}{2}=Q_{0}^{\pi^{\star}}(s_{0},a_{0})`$.
    Therefore,

    |  |  |  |
    |----|----|----|
    |  |
    ``` math
    \mathbb{E}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}[A_{h}^{\hat{\pi}}(s_{h},a_{h})]\approx\mathbb{E}_{a_{h}\sim\pi^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{h})}[A_{h}^{\pi^{\star}}(s_{h},a_{h})]=0,
    ``` |  |

    where the last equality follows from the definition of
    $`A_{h}^{\pi}`$.

Following steps in
[Section C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Proof of ‣ Appendix C Theoretical Proofs ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we obtain the approximate upper bound by adding $`|\Delta|`$ to the
theoretical bound.

To assess the impact of $`|\Delta|`$, we performed an ablation using the
step-by-step DPSDP variant in
[Section E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Empirical Impact of 𝑄-Value Estimation ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
which uses $`Q^{\pi_{2}}_{1}`$ in the DPO-style loss. The results showed
no significant performance gain, indicating that $`|\Delta|`$ has
minimal effect. For simplicity and efficiency, we use the original
version in the main paper.

## Appendix D Implementation Details

### D.1 Preliminary Training

As described in
[Section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Preliminary Training ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we begin by supervised fine-tuning the model to initialize the critic
for providing effective feedback and the actor for refining previous
answers. To acquire high-quality SFT dataset, we generate first-turn
responses by rolling out the reference policies, exposing errors that a
learner actor might make. An oracle model then generates feedback and
corresponding refined answers, demonstrating expected behavior for
critic and actor. After this initial stage, we proceed with DPSDP from
the boosted model.

In experiments, we use a subset of mathematical problems from
OpenMathInstruct-2 \[[Toshniwal et al., 2025](#bib.bib68)\] and sample
diverse first-turn answers with the base models
Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. To generate
high-quality feedback and refined answers, we employ capable models
Mistral-Large-Instruct-2411 and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, to demonstrate
how to evaluate and improve initial responses. After filtering (e.g.,
deduplicating problems and removing degraded answers), we obtain a final
dataset of 381K samples for supervised fine-tuning. We then fine-tune
the base models separately: the critic is trained on feedback
generation, while the actor is trained on refining answers. Both DPSDP
and baseline methods are subsequently trained on these fine-tuned
models.

### D.2 Benchmarks

(1) MATH 500\[[Hendrycks et al., 2021b](#bib.bib25)\]consists of
problems from mathematics competitions, including the AMC 10, AMC 12,
AIME, etc. The dataset covers diverse mathematical topics, including
algebra, geometry, statistics, number theory, linear algebra, and
calculus. Following [Lightman et al. \[2023\]](#bib.bib39), we augment
the MATH training set with 4500 problems from the test set and report
results on the remaining 500 problems, denoted as MATH 500. (2)
GSM8K\[[Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib10)\]includes 1319
grade-school-level math word problems, which are generally simpler than
those in MATH. (3) MMLU-Pro Math\[[Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib73)\]is a
mathematical subset of MMLU-Pro, a challenging multi-task benchmark. It
consists of 1351 multiple choice questions augmented from TheoremQA
\[[Chen et al., 2023](#bib.bib6)\], SciBench \[[Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib71)\], and original MMLU \[[Hendrycks et al.,
2021a](#bib.bib24)\]. (4) Olympiad Bench\[[He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23)\]is an Olympiad-level scientific benchmark, containing
674 open-ended text-only mathematical problems in English, covering
algebra, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory.

### D.3 Training Hyperparameters

For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we experimented with learning rates of
$`1\times 10^{-6}`$, $`5\times 10^{-6}`$, and $`1\times 10^{-5}`$,
selecting $`1\times 10^{-6}`$ for Llama-based models and
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$ for Ministral- and Qwen-based models. Base models
were trained on the SFT dataset for 1 epoch, using gradient accumulation
steps of 64 and a per-device train batch size of 1 on 4$`\times`$H100
80GB GPUs.

For direct preference optimization (DPO), we tested learning rates of
$`2\times 10^{-7}`$ and $`4\times 10^{-7}`$, choosing
$`2\times 10^{-7}`$ for Ministral-based actor and critic, Llama-based
actor, and Qwen-based actor, and $`4\times 10^{-7}`$ for Llama- and
Qwen-based critics. For the KL coefficient $`\beta`$, we evaluated
values of 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0, selecting 0.1 for all actor model training,
1.0 for Ministral-8B-Instruct-based critic (trained for 1 epoch), and
0.1 for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-based critic (trained for 2 epochs) and
Qwen2.5-3B-based critic (trained for 3 epochs). Same as in SFT, we used
gradient accumulation steps of 64 and a per-device train batch size of 1
on 4$`\times`$H100 80GB GPUs.

The non-generative critic was trained with a learning rate of
$`1\times 10^{-6}`$ for 1 epoch.

### D.4 Inference Hyperparameters

All evaluations were performed with a temperature ($`T`$) of 0, except
for self-consistency (maj5@turn1), where we set $`T=0.5`$. To generate
dataset used in the preliminary training phase (SFT), reference models
(Ministral-8B-Instruct-2410 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) generated
first-turn answers with $`T=0.8`$. Oracle models
(Mistral-Large-Instruct-2411 and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) then produced
feedback and refined answers with $`T=0`$. In the data collection stage
of
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Reduction of Cross-Entropy Loss to DPO Loss ‣ 3.3 Practical Algorithm ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
policies were sampled with $`T=1.0`$ to ensure diverse responses.

### D.5 Codebase

We adapted code from TRL \[[von Werra et al., 2020](#bib.bib69)\] for
both SFT and DPO training. The non-generative critic was trained using
the Hugging Face Transformers framework \[[Wolf et al.,
2020](#bib.bib76)\] with a customized loss function. For inference, we
utilized the vLLM offline engine \[[Kwon et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)\] and
adapted scripts from [Xiong et al. \[2024\]](#bib.bib82). Evaluation
code was adapted from [Yang et al. \[2024a\]](#bib.bib84), [Grattafiori
et al. \[2024\]](#bib.bib18) to compare LLM-generated answers with
ground-truth solution.

## Appendix E Additional Results

### E.1 Answer Improvement Over Turns

The training process of DPSDP involves single-step refinement rather
than multi-turn enhancement. Despite this discrepancy between training-
and test-time conditions, we find that DPSDP effectively enables models
to improve accuracy over multiple turns. In
[Fig. 3](#A5.F3 "In E.1 Answer Improvement Over Turns ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we plot the per-turn accuracy, majority voting accuracy, and
pass@t-$`k`$ accuracies on MATH 500 and GSM8K. For this section only, we
do not consider questions with no more than two correct responses as
incorrect, which is adopted in
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experimental Evaluation ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection").
The results show a general increase in accuracy as the number of
refinements grows, with models steadily improving majority voting
performance over successive turns. Additionally, the increasing
pass1@turn-$`k`$ scores indicate that models are progressively solving
problems they previously could not, demonstrating the effectiveness of
iterative refinement.

Figure 3: Various metrics under different turns. Accuracies improve as
the number of refinements increases. The rising pass1@turn-$`k`$ scores
indicate that iterative refinement enables models to solve previously
unsolved problems. Note that the decrease in maj1@t2 accuracy arises
from the requirement that both responses (2 out of 2) must be correct to
count toward maj1@t2.

We further analyze how the proportion of responses that change in
correctness evolves throughout the multi-turn refinement process.
[Table 4](#A5.T4 "In E.1 Answer Improvement Over Turns ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
reports results using Ministral-based models on the MATH 500 dataset. We
focus on the fraction of responses transitioning from incorrect to
correct, denoted $`\Delta^{i\rightarrow c}`$, and from correct to
incorrect, denoted $`\Delta^{c\rightarrow i}`$, at each refinement step.
Notably, $`\Delta^{i\rightarrow c}`$ consistently exceeds
$`\Delta^{c\rightarrow i}`$, indicating that the refinement process is
generally beneficial. Interestingly, both $`\Delta^{i\rightarrow c}`$
and $`\Delta^{c\rightarrow i}`$ decline over successive iterations,
suggesting an initial phase of active correction followed by
stabilization in later stages. The consistently low level of
$`\Delta^{c\rightarrow i}`$ suggest that over-refinement is not a
significant concern in practice. However, to further eliminate the
possibilities of over-refinement, we propose monitoring performance on a
validation set at each refinement step and stopping early if accuracy
begins to decline as a potential solution.

### E.2 Necessity of Preliminary Training Phase

As detailed in
[Section 3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Preliminary Training ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
our algorithm begins with models that have been fine-tuned to either
utilize or provide feedback. To assess the necessity of this preliminary
training, we conduct an ablation study by removing this phase and
applying DPSDP directly to base models. The results, shown in
[Table 5](#A5.T5 "In E.2 Necessity of Preliminary Training Phase ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
indicate that this fine-tuning step is essential for enabling the actor
and critic models to follow instructions effectively. Without it,
applying DPSDP yields negligible performance gains with additional
response attempts. For instance, the models achieve only 53.8% accuracy
on MATH 500—an improvement of just 1.2% over a single-response baseline.
In contrast, incorporating the preliminary training leads to a 5.0%
absolute gain in accuracy. These findings are consistent with previous
work \[[Chu et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)\], underscoring the importance of
instruction-following capabilities in models used as starting points for
RL training.

### E.3 Empirical Impact of $`Q`$-Value Estimation

In
[Section 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Practical Algorithm ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection"),
we present the development of a practical DPSDP approach, leveraging
$`\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}`$ to approximate $`Q`$-values that are otherwise
infeasible or computationally costly to obtain. We are especially
interested in investigating our approximation of
$`Q_{1}^{{\widehat{\pi}}_{2}}(s_{1},a_{1})`$, the $`Q`$-values for the
feedback step. To evaluate the impact of it, we conduct experiments on a
smaller dataset primarily consisting of augmented problems from MATH. We
first replicate the training process from
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Reduction of Cross-Entropy Loss to DPO Loss ‣ 3.3 Practical Algorithm ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
on this dataset, using $`\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}`$ for estimation and
combining training across all turns into a single step for each agent,
which we refer to as unified training. In contrast, we implement a
step-by-step training procedure based on
[Algorithm 1](#alg1 "In 3.1 Algorithm Development ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection")
with a DPO loss, with each turn being trained separately. We denote this
approach as step-by-step training. Specifically, we first use
$`\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}`$ to sample $`n`$ second-turn answers, which are
then used to construct a DPO dataset for actor training, yielding an
intermediate actor model $`{{\widehat{\pi}}}_{2}^{a}`$. Next, we sample
diverse feedback from the base critic and use
$`{{\widehat{\pi}}}_{2}^{a}`$, instead of $`\pi_{\mathsf{ref}}`$ as in
unified training, to generate refined answers based on this feedback,
obtaining an accurate value of $`Q_{1}^{{{\widehat{\pi}}}_{2}^{a}}`$. We
then conduct DPO training on the critic, producing a refined critic
model $`{{\widehat{\pi}}}_{1}^{c}`$. Finally, we improve the actor’s
first-turn responses based on $`{{\widehat{\pi}}}_{2}^{a}`$, following
the same approach as in
[Algorithm 2](#alg2 "In Reduction of Cross-Entropy Loss to DPO Loss ‣ 3.3 Practical Algorithm ‣ 3 DPSDP: Direct Policy Search by Dynamic Programming ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection").
To ensure broad exposure to different problems, we use three distinct
problem sets at each stage of step-by-step training, each matching the
size of the dataset used in unified training. We evaluate both methods
on MATH 500 using Llama-based models, as shown in
[Table 6](#A5.T6 "In E.3 Empirical Impact of 𝑄-Value Estimation ‣ Appendix E Additional Results ‣ Reinforce LLM Reasoning through Multi-Agent Reflection").
Notably, we find that the policy trained via unified training
outperforms the step-by-step approach, suggesting both the accuracy of
our estimation strategy and the potential advantage of jointly learning
answers alongside their refinements.

|------------------------|----------|---------|---------|
| Approach               | MATH 500 |         |         |
|                        |  p1@t1   |  m1@t5  |  p1@t5  |
| Llama-3.1 Unified      |  54.4    |  55.2   |  59.2   |
| Llama-3.1 Step-by-Step |          |         |         |
| + Trained on $`a_{2}`$ |  53.0    |  54.2   |  58.6   |
| + Trained on $`a_{1}`$ |  53.0    |  54.0   |  58.8   |
| + Trained on $`a_{0}`$ |  52.6    |  54.2   |  59.0   |
````
